title: Work in the Gig Economy
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Not long ago, a job meant a contract with one employer, a regular salary and a pension at the end. Today, millions of people earn money in a different way: by taking short pieces of work, called gigs, through digital platforms. They drive passengers, deliver meals, translate documents or design logos, and they are paid for each task rather than by the hour or the month. This arrangement is known as the gig economy, and by some estimates it already involves more than a hundred million workers around the world.

Supporters point first to freedom. A gig worker chooses when to work, and can stop at any time to study, to look after a child or to rest. For people who find it hard to get a regular job, such as students, migrants or those with disabilities, a platform may be the only opening. Customers benefit too, as services that once required a telephone call and a long wait can now be ordered in seconds, often at lower prices. For many young people, a few hours of gig work is also a first step towards a career.

Critics, however, argue that the freedom is smaller than it appears. Most platforms set the price of each task, and workers who refuse too many offers may find that they receive fewer in the future. Because gig workers are usually classed as self-employed, they do not receive paid holidays, sick pay or a pension, and they must pay for their own vehicles, phones and insurance. A study of delivery riders in one European city found that, after these costs were deducted, many earned less than the legal minimum wage.

The legal position is still unclear. In 2021, the UK Supreme Court ruled that drivers working for a large taxi app were 'workers', not self-employed, and were therefore entitled to a minimum wage and paid leave. Courts in other countries have reached different conclusions, and some governments have written new laws instead. Professor Samir Haddad, an economist, believes that a third category, between employee and self-employed, would be fairer than forcing every worker into one of the two existing boxes.

Algorithms add a further complication. A platform's software decides which worker receives a task, rates workers on the basis of customer reviews and, in some cases, removes workers from the platform without a human being involved. Workers often complain that they cannot find out why a decision was taken, and have no one to whom they can appeal. Some countries are therefore considering laws that would give workers the right to an explanation, and the right to take their ratings with them if they move to another platform.

It would be wrong, though, to see the gig economy only as a problem. Surveys in several countries suggest that many workers value the flexibility and would not exchange it for a fixed timetable. The difficulty is that flexibility and security are hard to combine. Some platforms have begun to offer insurance or a guaranteed minimum for hours worked, but critics say that such schemes cover only a small share of workers, and that they are often withdrawn when the platform faces competition.

Whatever the outcome of these debates, the pattern of work is likely to keep changing. Automation may replace some tasks, while creating others that nobody has yet imagined. The most useful response, many economists argue, is not to resist the change but to ensure that the protections once linked to a single job, such as health care and pensions, are attached to the worker instead. How quickly governments will agree to do so remains to be seen.
